english: How does one show this more directly?
topic: Three short notes: questions on the discriminant of a quadratic form built from the roots of an algebraic equation (the equation with real roots in lambda), a question on directly proving regularity of solutions of differential equations other than Laplace's, and the problem of counting the possible configurations of n circles in the plane.

triage.modern_statement: The note is short and its context is only partly clear. The most likely reading attaches it to the regularity note on this page. In modern terms the question would be: for elliptic PDEs other than Laplace's equation (for example Euler–Lagrange equations of regular variational problems with analytic integrand), how can one prove directly that every sufficiently regular solution is analytic, rather than relying on special tools that only work for Laplace's equation, such as explicit Poisson-type integral formulas? A less likely reading is that 'dies' refers to the discriminant note on the same page. That note seems to ask for a more direct proof that the λ-equation has real roots, for example by writing the discriminant as a sum of squares. I did not search for or check that second reading.
triage.answered_by: If the regularity reading is right, this is closely tied to Hilbert's 19th problem (1900). Partial answer: S. Bernstein, 1904 thesis (C^3 solutions are analytic; n=2, later extended to general dimension). Full solution: E. De Giorgi (1956–57) and J. Nash (1957–58), independently, by proving Hölder continuity of first derivatives; J. Moser later gave a new formulation of the proof (the De Giorgi–Nash–Moser theory).

evidence.claim: Hilbert's 19th problem (1900) asks whether solutions of regular problems in the calculus of variations are always analytic, and Hilbert framed it as a regularity problem for elliptic PDEs with analytic coefficients.

Bernstein (1904) answered it positively for C^3 solutions; De Giorgi (1956, 1957) and Nash (1957, 1958) independently closed the remaining gap by proving that first derivatives are Hölder continuous, which completed the solution.

Timeline: in 1904 Bernstein proved that analyticity follows from C^3 regularity (n=2); in 1957 De Giorgi and Nash independently solved the problem. These steps make up the De Giorgi–Nash–Moser theory.
Moser later gave a new formulation of the proof, and De Giorgi–Nash–Moser techniques are still applied to degenerate parabolic and integral operators and to partial regularity for Navier–Stokes.

triage.why: The word 'direkter' ('more directly') matches the page's note about directly proving regularity for differential equations other than Laplace's. That question is essentially what Hilbert later published as Problem 19 in 1900; the 20th problem, on boundary value problems, is related. It was settled by Bernstein in 1904 and by De Giorgi and Nash in 1956–58. Regularity theory in the De Giorgi–Nash–Moser tradition is still an active research area (a 2025 arXiv survey on quantitative De Giorgi methods is one example). Confidence is only medium because the diary text does not show which statement 'dies' refers to. It could instead belong to the discriminant/real-roots note, which I did not investigate, so that reading has no sources behind it.
